newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian coalition sets emergency meeting on bank.
newsitem.headline: Austrian coalition sets emergency meeting on bank.

text.p: Austria's fractious coalition parties, split over how to privatise the country's second biggest bank, agreed on one thing on Thursday -- to bring forward an emergency government meeting on the row to Saturday.

The controversial selloff of Creditanstalt-Bankverein has plunged the government of Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party into its biggest crisis since a snap election in December 1995.
An emergency meeting of coalition leaders, tentatively set for Monday, was swiftly rescheduled for Saturday afternoon, Social Democrat sources said.

Political analysts said the Social Democrats would try to engineer a deal at the meeting to solve differences over the sale of Creditanstalt -- once the bankers of the Habsburg imperial family and still considered a fiefdom of the conservatives.

The People's Party objects to the prospect of Creditanstalt being taken over by rival Bank Austria, which is indirectly controlled by the Social Democrat-dominated City of Vienna and part-owned by the state.

The People's Party, led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel, would see such a move as an attempt by the Social Democrats to consolidate their control over Austria's banking industry at the conservatives' expense.
The conservatives would like to see the bank sold to an international consortium led by Italian-controlled insurer EA-Generali.
But several banking sources suggested that Bank Austria had more or less clinched the sale as EA-Generali appeared unlikely to top Bank Austria's 16.8 billion schilling ($1.52 billion) offer.
Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima, speaking at a conference of his party in the southern spa town of Bad Tatzmannsdorf, said he was bound by European Union law to accept the highest bid.

"It's very difficult at the moment to understand what exactly our coalition partners want," a visibly frustrated Klima said. "They claim we violated our coalition agreement, but they can't name one example."
Klima said he had informed Schuessel in writing last September that he would only accept the highest offer and that Schuessel was in agreement.

"I'm a consensus-orientated individual....but I'm not prepared to be driven into something that runs counter to EU law -- and I'm certainly not prepared to forego three to four billion schillings," the finance minister added.

The deadline for final offers for Creditanstalt expires at 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) on Friday but Schuessel's conservatives have cautioned Klima not to make a decision before an emergency session of parliament next Tuesday.

The Social Democrats are well aware that their conservative partners have held a series of talks with far-right opposition leader Joerg Haider over the sell-off ahead of the special parliamentary session.

Rightwinger Haider has made strong electoral gains in recent years but has been frozen out of power by the coalition alliance. He told a news conference the far right and conservatives had found common ground on a number of points regarding the sale of the bank but declined to give details. ($1=11.05 Schilling)
